title: Bonhoeffer's prison questions
hookLine: in prison he asked who Christ is for us today

lines: WHO IS CHRIST, FOR US TODAY?
cards: A prison cell in Berlin. Letters go out with the help of guards willing to carry them.
The prisoner is Dietrich Bonhoeffer, the Lutheran pastor this path met earlier, held by the Nazi regime and connected to the resistance against it. Outside, the war goes on.
Inside, he writes to his friend Eberhard Bethge, and in one of those letters puts down a question he can't stop turning over: who is Christ really, for us today? Not a question for a seminar.
A question from a man who didn't know if he'd see the outside again.

teach.h: WHO IS CHRIST FOR US TODAY?
teach.b: Bonhoeffer wasn't asking what Christ meant for people long ago, or what the creeds say in the abstract. He was asking what Christ means for a world where people no longer felt they needed religion to explain things.

teach.h: AT THE CENTER, NOT THE EDGES
teach.b: In his letters he tried out bold phrases, like religionless Christianity, and he warned against using God as a stopgap: a God who only shows up at the edges, where our knowledge runs out or our strength gives way.
God, he wrote, should be found at the center of life: in strength as well as weakness, in health and not only in a crisis.
In notes for a book he never finished, he called Jesus the man for others, and said the church is only the church when it exists for others. He didn't live to work it out.

The Nazi regime executed him before the war ended, and the questions stayed open. Christians still read them differently. Some hear a call to a quieter, more worldly faith, lived out in plain service.
Others point out that in another letter he named prayer and doing what is right as the heart of being a Christian in his time, and hear a call to costly discipleship. The question itself is old.

teach.h: BUT WHOM SAY YE THAT I AM?
teach.b: Near Caesarea Philippi, Jesus asked his own disciples: "But whom say ye that I am?" Bonhoeffer heard it again, in a cell, with the world on fire around him.

how: Bonhoeffer's prison letters, published after his death, are read in study groups, sermons and retreats; some Christians keep his question in front of them as a way of examining how their faith meets daily life.

games.why: he asked who Christ really is, for us today, and called Jesus the man for others. the question was never finished; he was executed before the war ended.

practice: Let Bonhoeffer's question sit with you, then bring it closer: who is Christ, for this week, in the life you actually have?

If you follow Jesus, notice what answer comes and what answer you wish would come; if you don't, ask what his life seems to mean to the people you know who do. There's no need to land anywhere; just keep the question company.
